content: 1. If test results for syphilis are negative and presumptive treatment is not provided, it is recommended to repeat the tests after four weeks, in accordance with the World Health Organization (WHO) syphilis guidelines. 2. Efforts are currently being made to develop point-of-care tests (POCTs) for other sexually transmitted infections (STIs). These tests aim to enhance the syndromic management of symptomatic cases and improve the detection of asymptomatic infections. 3. The drug regimens and dosages used for syndromic case management and presumptive STI treatment should be guided by national protocols and guidelines. 4. Additional information can be found in the WHO guidelines on the management of gonorrhea, chlamydia, syphilis, and herpes simplex virus, published in 2016. These guidelines provide detailed recommendations for the diagnosis and treatment of these infections. 5. In settings where laboratory testing is unavailable or inaccessible for certain populations, requiring children or adolescents to return for test results before receiving treatment may reduce treatment uptake. Studies included in the review indicate a high rate of loss to follow-up among survivors in subsequent visits. 6. Conversely, in cases of ongoing abuse or where laboratory testing is feasible, it may be critical to conduct testing prior to initiating treatment to ensure appropriate care. 7. References to studies and guidelines include: Lokoko Roka J et al., discussing standardized care for survivors of sexual violence in conflict and post-conflict areas in the Democratic Republic of Congo (PLOS ONE, 2011). Argent AC et al., addressing sexually transmitted diseases in children and evidence of sexual abuse (Child Abuse Negl., 1995). Ononge S et al., examining the clinical presentation and management of sexually assaulted females at Mulago Hospital, Kampala, Uganda (Afr Health Sci., 2005). Nunthanid S., analyzing management outcomes for survivors of sexual assault at Photharam Hospital (Srinagarind Med J., 2008). Oshikata CT et al., reporting on emergency care for women following sexual assault and six-month post-aggression follow-up (Cad Saude Publica, 2005, in Portuguese). 8. WHO guidelines for the treatment of gonorrhea, chlamydia, syphilis, and genital herpes simplex virus are available online for further reference.
